topics.title: Fick's second law and the error-function solution (Q14–Q24) **[HIGHEST-YIELD]**

questions.text: Diffusion is the thread connecting earlier chapters because it is what:

statements.text: lets homogenisation (Ch. 3) even out segregation
lets an edge dislocation climb (Ch. 5)
lets a Cottrell atmosphere form (Ch. 6)
controls how fast a precipitate coarsens during ageing (Ch. 7)

questions.keyExplanation: All four connections are correct — this is why diffusion closes the course.
questions.concise: Diffusion drives homogenisation, climb, Cottrell atmospheres and precipitate coarsening — all four chapter links are correct.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: homogenisation (Ch. 3) is diffusion evening out segregation (t ∝ distance²).
- Item 2 — TRUE: an edge dislocation climbs by absorbing/emitting vacancies (Ch. 5 Q27).
- Item 3 — TRUE: a Cottrell atmosphere forms by solute *diffusing* to a dislocation (Ch. 6).
- Item 4 — TRUE: precipitate coarsening during ageing (Ostwald ripening) is diffusion-controlled
  (Ch. 7 Q35).

All four are correct. **Diffusion is the thread that closes the course** — it is the mechanism
behind a named phenomenon in almost every earlier chapter. That is why it is usually examined as
a cross-chapter "link" question.

questions.text: The *vacancy mechanism* operates as:

options.label: a
options.text: a substitutional atom jumps into an adjacent vacant site

options.label: b
options.text: a small solute atom hops directly between interstitial voids with no vacancy needed

options.label: c
options.text: an atom moves along a grain boundary only

options.label: d
options.text: an atom moves by dislocation glide

questions.keyExplanation: [P2] Vacancy mechanism = substitutional atom hops into an adjacent vacancy.
questions.concise: Vacancy mechanism = substitutional atom hops into a neighbouring vacancy.
questions.detailed:
In the **vacancy mechanism**, a substitutional atom moves by jumping into an
adjacent **vacant lattice site**. The vacancy is essential — without one to jump into, a
substitutional atom cannot move.
- (b) describes the **interstitial** mechanism (Q3).
- (c) grain-boundary diffusion is a *short-circuit path* (Q32), not this mechanism.
- (d) dislocation glide is plastic deformation, not diffusion.

**[P2] rule:** *substitutional → needs a vacancy; interstitial → needs no vacancy.*

questions.text: The *interstitial mechanism* operates as:

options.label: a
options.text: a substitutional atom hops into a vacancy

options.label: b
options.text: an atom moves through an intermetallic compound

options.label: c
options.text: an atom moves only at grain boundaries

options.label: d
options.text: a small solute atom (C, N, H) hops directly from one interstitial void to a neighbouring one — no vacancy required

questions.keyExplanation: [P2] Interstitial mechanism = small atom (C, N, H) hops between voids, no vacancy needed.
questions.concise: Interstitial mechanism = small atom (C, N, H) hops between voids, no vacancy needed.
questions.detailed: The interstitial mechanism is a small solute atom hopping directly between neighbouring interstitial voids without requiring a vacancy. **(d)** is correct. Option (a) is the vacancy mechanism; (b) and (c) do not describe ordinary interstitial diffusion.

questions.text: The vacancy mechanism's rate is limited by:

statements.text: the energy to move the atom
the equilibrium vacancy concentration available to jump into
the applied stress only
the grain size only

questions.keyExplanation: 1 and 2 — atom-move energy **and** vacancy availability both limit the rate.
questions.concise: The rate needs both a move energy and available vacancies — not stress or grain size.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: the atom must overcome a migration energy barrier to move.
- Item 2 — TRUE: it must also have an equilibrium **vacancy** to jump into — the vacancy
  concentration (exp(−Q_v/kT), Ch. 5 Q7) sets how often a jump is possible.
- Item 3 — FALSE: applied stress does not control lattice diffusion.
- Item 4 — FALSE: grain size affects *short-circuit* diffusion (Q33), not the bulk mechanism's
  rate-limiting steps.

The vacancy mechanism needs **two** energies in series — the energy to *make* a vacancy and the
energy to *move* the atom into it. This is why Q_d (Ch. 8) is larger than the migration energy
alone.

questions.text: Which statement(s) contrasting interstitial and vacancy diffusion is/are correct?

statements.text: Interstitial diffusion needs no vacancy.
Its activation energy is much lower.
It is orders of magnitude faster than substitutional diffusion at the same temperature.
Interstitial diffusion is slower than substitutional diffusion.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 reverses the truth. [P2]
questions.concise: Interstitial needs no vacancy, has lower Q_d, and is orders of magnitude faster — it is NOT slower.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: interstitial diffusion needs no vacancy.
- Item 2 — TRUE: its activation energy is much lower (no vacancy-formation term).
- Item 3 — TRUE: it is orders of magnitude faster than substitutional diffusion at the same
  temperature.
- Item 4 — FALSE: this reverses the truth — interstitial diffusion is *faster*, not slower.

Item 4 is the [P2] inversion. The reason for the speed difference is structural: a small
interstitial atom is already in a gap and only needs to squeeze past its neighbours, whereas a
substitutional atom must both create/find a vacancy *and* push past a full shell of neighbours.

questions.text: This speed difference explains why:

statements.text: carburizing is practical on a furnace timescale
homogenising a substitutional alloy takes hours to days
both processes take exactly the same time
nitriding is impossible

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2 correct; item 3 is false.
questions.concise: Fast interstitial diffusion makes carburizing practical; slow substitutional diffusion makes homogenising take hours to days — the times are not the same.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: carburizing is practical on a furnace timescale *because* carbon (interstitial)
  diffuses fast.
- Item 2 — TRUE: homogenising a substitutional alloy takes hours to days because substitutional
  diffusion is slow.
- Item 3 — FALSE: they emphatically do **not** take the same time — that is the whole point.
- Item 4 — FALSE: nitriding (nitrogen into steel surface) is standard industrial practice.

Item 3 contradicts items 1 and 2. The industrial significance: **the mechanism choice dictates
the process timescale** — hours for a carburizing case, days for a homogenising anneal.

questions.assertion: Interstitial diffusion of carbon in steel is orders of magnitude faster than substitutional diffusion of, say, nickel in steel at the same temperature.
questions.reason: The interstitial mechanism requires no vacancy and has a much lower activation energy.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true.
questions.concise: No vacancy needed + lower Q_d is exactly why interstitial C in steel is far faster than substitutional Ni.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: interstitial diffusion of carbon in steel is orders of magnitude faster than
  substitutional diffusion of, say, nickel in steel at the same temperature.
- R is TRUE: the interstitial mechanism requires no vacancy and has a much lower activation
  energy.

R correctly explains A. The Arrhenius form (Q25) makes the argument quantitative: a lower Q_d
means a larger exp(−Q_d/RT), hence a much larger D — and because the dependence is exponential,
even a modest Q_d difference produces an *orders-of-magnitude* rate difference.

questions.text: Tracer measurements in dilute α-iron show the following qualitative diffusivity ranking at the same temperature. Combine the data with the usual site-occupancy model to identify the most consistent mechanism pairing.
tableRows: Fast relative to substitutional alloying atoms
Much slower under comparable dilute conditions

options.label: a
options.text: C, N and H typically diffuse interstitially; Ni, Cu and Mn typically move by vacancy-mediated substitutional diffusion.

options.label: b
options.text: C and N diffuse by vacancy exchange, while Ni and Cu move interstitially because metallic bonding is stronger.

options.label: c
options.text: Both groups use the same vacancy mechanism; the diffusivity contrast is explained only by atomic mass.

options.label: d
options.text: Both groups use interstitial paths; the contrast arises only from different equilibrium concentrations.

questions.keyExplanation: The rapid interstitial solutes C, N and H are small enough to move between lattice sites, while substitutional metallic solutes such as Ni, Cu and Mn typically require vacancy exchanges. Diffusivity alone is not a universal diagnostic, but the observed ranking is consistent with this common mechanism pairing.
questions.concise: Small interstitial solutes diffuse quickly; substitutional metallic solutes generally use vacancy exchange.
questions.detailed: C, N and H can occupy interstitial sites and move between them without waiting for a substitutional vacancy exchange. Ni, Cu and Mn occupy substitutional sites and typically move through vacancy-mediated jumps. The table’s relative rates are consistent with this distinction, though exact diffusivities also depend on temperature, concentration, phase and activation energies.

questions.text: Fick's first law is:
questions.keyExplanation: J = −D dC/dx.
questions.concise: J = −D dC/dx.
questions.detailed: Fick's first law is J = −D dC/dx, so **(d)** is correct. Option (a) has the wrong sign; (b) is not a flux law; and (c) is the spatial-derivative term appearing in Fick's second law, not the first law.

questions.text: In Fick's first law, J is:

options.label: a
options.text: the flux — atoms per unit area per unit time

questions.keyExplanation: J = flux (atoms per unit area per unit time).
questions.concise: J = flux (atoms per unit area per unit time).
questions.detailed:
J is the **flux** — the number of atoms (or moles) crossing a unit area per unit
time. Units: atoms·m⁻²·s⁻¹ or mol·m⁻²·s⁻¹.
- (b) the activation energy is Q_d.
- (c) the grain-boundary energy is γ_gb.
- (d) heat flux is q (units W/m²) — a different quantity entirely, though mathematically
  analogous (Fourier's law mirrors Fick's first law).

questions.text: The negative sign in Fick's first law indicates that:

options.label: b
options.text: diffusion runs **down** the concentration gradient, from high to low concentration

questions.keyExplanation: [P3] The minus sign means diffusion is *down* the gradient. Do not read "minus" as "heat".
questions.concise: The minus sign = down the gradient. Do not read "minus" as "heat".
questions.detailed: The negative sign in J = −D dC/dx means flux runs down the concentration gradient, from high concentration toward low concentration. **(b)** is correct. The sign specifies direction; it does not describe heat or whether concentration increases with time.

questions.text: Fick's first law applies under:

options.label: d
options.text: steady state — a concentration profile that is not changing with time

questions.keyExplanation: Fick's first law = steady state.
questions.concise: Fick's first law = steady state (∂C/∂t = 0).
questions.detailed: Fick's first law is used for steady-state diffusion, where the concentration profile is time-independent. **(d)** is correct. Options (a) and (b) describe transient/non-steady conditions; (c) is equilibrium, where the net flux would be zero.

questions.text: The standard application of Fick's first law is:

options.label: a
options.text: steady-state permeation through a thin plate or membrane held at fixed, different concentrations on either face (e.g. hydrogen gas through a metal wall)

questions.keyExplanation: Steady-state membrane permeation (H₂ through a metal wall) is the classic first-law case. [P2] — contrast with carburizing, which is a *second-law* problem.
questions.concise: The classic first-law application = steady-state membrane permeation (H₂ through a wall).
questions.detailed:
The textbook first-law setup:
```
membrane of thickness L
C = C₁ fixed on one face, C = C₂ fixed on the other
after a start-up transient, ∂C/∂t = 0 → steady state
J = −D(C₂ − C₁)/L = D(C₁ − C₂)/L
```
Hydrogen permeation through a steel pressure-vessel wall is the standard industrial example.
- (b) the carburizing depth profile is a **second-law** problem (Q16).
- (c), (d) are unrelated.
**[P2] the discriminator:** if the profile is *fixed in time* → first law; if it *changes with
time* → second law.

questions.text: Fick's second law is:
questions.keyExplanation: ∂C/∂t = D ∂²C/∂x².
questions.concise: ∂C/∂t = D ∂²C/∂x².
questions.detailed: Fick's second law for constant D in one dimension is ∂C/∂t = D ∂²C/∂x². **(b)** is correct. Option (a) is Fick's first law; (c) has an incorrect sign; and (d) is not Fick's second law.

questions.text: Fick's second law describes:

options.label: d
options.text: non-steady-state diffusion, where concentration at a given point changes with time

questions.keyExplanation: Second law = non-steady state.
questions.concise: Second law = non-steady state (C changes with time at a point).
questions.detailed: Fick's second law describes non-steady-state diffusion, where concentration at a point changes with time. **(d)** is correct. Option (a) describes the steady-state setting associated with the first law; (b) is heat conduction; and (c) is phase equilibrium.

questions.text: For a semi-infinite solid initially at uniform concentration C₀, with its surface suddenly held at a fixed higher concentration C_s, the solution is:
questions.keyExplanation: (C_x − C₀)/(C_s − C₀) = 1 − erf( x/(2√(Dt)) ). Note the **1 − erf**, a favourite distractor.
questions.concise: (C_x − C₀)/(C_s − C₀) = 1 − erf( x/(2√(Dt)) ) — note the **1 − erf**.
questions.detailed: For a semi-infinite solid with a fixed surface concentration, the solution is (C_x − C₀)/(C_s − C₀) = 1 − erf[x/(2√(Dt))]. **(d)** is correct. Option (a) omits the leading 1 −; (b) is an exponential profile, not this boundary-condition solution; and (c) is not the solution.

questions.text: In the error-function solution, "erf" is:

options.label: d
options.text: the Gaussian error function — a tabulated, standard mathematical function

questions.keyExplanation: erf is the tabulated Gaussian error function.
questions.concise: erf is the tabulated Gaussian error function.
questions.detailed: The function erf is the standard Gaussian error function, defined by erf(z) = (2/√π)∫₀ᶻ exp(−u²)du. **(d)** is correct. It is a tabulated mathematical function, not an error in the derivation, activation energy or flux.

questions.text: A constant-surface-concentration solution is used for transient diffusion into a semi-infinite solid with uniform initial concentration $C_0$ and fixed surface concentration $C_s$. Which situations match these assumptions most closely?

statements.text: Carburizing a steel surface while the interior initially has a nearly uniform carbon concentration.
Nitriding a component when the surface nitrogen potential is maintained during treatment.
Semiconductor diffusion doping from a source that maintains an approximately fixed surface concentration.
Steady-state permeation through a finite-thickness membrane after the concentration profile has become linear.

questions.keyExplanation: Carburizing, nitriding and diffusion doping can be modeled with a maintained surface concentration and a transient semi-infinite-solid approximation. Steady-state permeation through a finite membrane instead uses a finite-domain steady-state concentration gradient.
questions.concise: The error-function solution models transient penetration into a semi-infinite solid, not a finite membrane already at steady state.
questions.detailed: Items 1–3 can be approximated by a fixed surface concentration while the initially uniform interior evolves in time. The semi-infinite assumption requires the diffusion front not yet to have reached the far boundary. Item 4 describes a finite membrane at steady state, where the concentration profile is already established and the appropriate model is different. Steady-state permeation is still a diffusion problem, commonly treated with Fick’s first law; the issue is its boundary conditions and time regime.

questions.text: Diffusion distance scales as:
questions.keyExplanation: Diffusion distance ∝ √(Dt).
questions.concise: Diffusion penetration depth scales as √(Dt).
questions.detailed: The characteristic diffusion distance scales as √(Dt), so **(b)** is correct. Options (a) and (d) omit the square root or place time incorrectly; (c) puts time in the denominator and has the wrong scaling.

questions.text: At a fixed temperature, doubling the required case depth needs:
questions.keyExplanation: Depth ∝ √t, so doubling depth needs 4× the time.
questions.concise: Depth ∝ √t, so doubling depth needs 4× the time.
questions.detailed:
```
depth ∝ √t   →   t ∝ depth²

doubling depth:  t_new ∝ (2d)² = 4d² = 4 × t_old
```
So **2× depth costs 4× time**.
- (a) 2× time would only give √2 × depth.
- (c), (d) are wrong.
This is the single most commonly mis-stated scaling in the whole course. **The shortcut to
memorise:** *2× depth = 4× time; 4× depth = 16× time.*

questions.text: **Worked example.** A steel part (C₀ = 0.05 wt% C) is carburized in an atmosphere holding the surface at C_s = 1.0 wt% C, with D = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s. The time needed to reach C_x = 0.4 wt% C at x = 0.6 mm is approximately:
questions.keyExplanation: See derivation below — 2.2 × 10⁴ s ≈ 6.1 h.
questions.detailed: The normalised concentration is (0.4 − 0.05)/(1.0 − 0.05) = 0.35/0.95 = 0.368. Thus erf(z) = 1 − 0.368 = 0.632, giving z ≈ 0.64 and t ≈ 2.2 × 10⁴ s. **(a)** is correct. The other options differ by factors of ten or one hundred.

questions.text: In the worked example of Q21, the value of z = x/(2√(Dt)) that satisfies the equation is approximately:
questions.detailed:
From Q21 Step 3: erf(z) = 0.632, and from the error-function table:
```
erf(0.60) = 0.6039
erf(0.65) = 0.6420
erf(0.64) ≈ 0.632   ✓
```
So z ≈ **0.64**.
- (a) 0.064 would give erf ≈ 0.071.
- (b) 0.36 would give erf ≈ 0.389.
- (d) 1.60 would give erf ≈ 0.976.
**Reading the table:** interpolate between the tabulated z values bracketing your erf(z) — that
is the whole skill being tested here.

questions.text: In the worked example of Q21, the intermediate step gives:
questions.concise: Normalised value 0.368 → erf(z) = 0.632.
questions.detailed:
```
(C_x − C₀)/(C_s − C₀) = (0.4 − 0.05)/(1.0 − 0.05) = 0.35/0.95 = 0.368
0.368 = 1 − erf(z)  →  erf(z) = 1 − 0.368 = 0.632
```
- (b) swaps the two numbers (puts 0.632 on the left) — the classic error of forgetting the
  "1 − " in the solution (Q16).
- (c) 0.40 would come from using C_x/C_s = 0.4/1.0, forgetting to normalise against C₀.
- (d) 1.0 would mean C_x = C_s — i.e. the surface, not x = 0.6 mm.
**Why (b) is the trap:** if you used the wrong form (C_x − C₀)/(C_s − C₀) = erf(z) from Q16
option (b), you would get exactly the numbers in (b) — the distractor catches the Q16 error
downstream.

questions.text: The concentration–depth profiles from the error-function solution at increasing diffusion time show that:

options.label: a
options.text: longer times push the same concentration level to greater depth

options.label: b
options.text: longer times pull the profile back toward the surface

options.label: c
options.text: the surface concentration falls with time

options.label: d
options.text: the profile is independent of time

questions.keyExplanation: Longer time → the same concentration is reached at greater depth.
questions.concise: Longer time → the same concentration reached at greater depth.
questions.detailed:
Since penetration depth ∝ √(Dt) (Q19), increasing t stretches the profile out
along the depth axis — every concentration level moves deeper.
- (b) is the reverse.
- (c) false — C_s is *held fixed* by the boundary condition (that is what makes it the erf case).
- (d) false — the profile is explicitly time-dependent via √(Dt).
This is the visual counterpart of Q20: the family of erf curves at increasing t all start at C_s
at x = 0 and fan out to the right.

questions.text: The Arrhenius form of the diffusion coefficient is:
questions.keyExplanation: D = D₀ exp(−Q_d/RT).
questions.concise: D = D₀ exp(−Q_d/RT).
questions.detailed: The Arrhenius relation for diffusion is D = D₀ exp(−Q_d/RT), so **(b)** is correct. A positive exponent would make D increase as temperature falls, contrary to thermally activated diffusion; the remaining options are not exponential Arrhenius forms.

questions.text: In the Arrhenius equation, D₀ is:
questions.keyExplanation: D₀ = pre-exponential constant. [P2]
questions.concise: D₀ = pre-exponential constant.
questions.detailed:
D₀ is the **pre-exponential (frequency) factor** — the value D would approach at
infinite temperature, and a measure of the attempt frequency and geometry of atomic jumps. It is
essentially temperature-independent.
- (b) Q_d is the activation energy (Q27).
- (c) R is the gas constant.
- (d) T is the absolute temperature.

questions.text: In the Arrhenius equation, Q_d is:
questions.keyExplanation: Q_d = activation energy for diffusion. [P2] — D₀ vs Q_d is a two-way confusion risk.
questions.concise: Q_d = activation energy for diffusion.
questions.detailed:
Q_d is the **activation energy** — the total energy barrier a diffusing atom must
overcome. For the vacancy mechanism this includes both the vacancy-formation energy and the
migration energy (Q4).
- (b) D₀ is the pre-exponential constant (Q26).
- (c) J is the flux.
- (d) d is the grain diameter.
**[P2] D₀ vs Q_d** is a two-way confusion risk — but they are easily separated by *units*:
D₀ has units of m²/s (a diffusivity), Q_d has units of J/mol or eV (an energy).

questions.text: On an Arrhenius plot of ln D versus 1/T, the slope is:
questions.keyExplanation: Slope of ln D vs 1/T = −Q_d/R.
questions.concise: Slope of ln D vs 1/T = −Q_d/R.
questions.detailed: Taking the natural logarithm gives ln D = ln D₀ − (Q_d/R)(1/T). Therefore the slope of ln D against 1/T is −Q_d/R, so **(d)** is correct. The intercept is ln D₀; the other options are not the slope.

questions.text: The Arrhenius plots below are fitted as $\ln D=\ln D_0-(Q_D/R)(1/T)$. Use the fitted slopes to compare the activation energies.

options.label: a
options.text: $Q_C\approx80\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $Q_{Ni}\approx249\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; carbon has the lower activation energy.

options.label: b
options.text: $Q_C\approx249\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $Q_{Ni}\approx80\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; carbon has the higher activation energy.

options.label: c
options.text: Both activation energies are about $8.3\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ because the slopes are dimensionless.

options.label: d
options.text: The activation energies cannot be compared from slope; only the intercept $\ln D_0$ determines $Q_D$.

questions.keyExplanation: The slope equals $-Q_D/R$, so $Q_D=R|\mathrm{slope}|$. Multiplying by $R=8.314\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$ gives approximately 80 kJ/mol for carbon and 249 kJ/mol for nickel.
questions.concise: Arrhenius slope magnitude is $Q_D/R$; the steeper nickel line therefore has the greater activation energy.
questions.detailed: For carbon, $Q_D=(8.314)(9.6\times10^3)\approx7.98\times10^4\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}=80\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. For nickel, $Q_D=(8.314)(3.0\times10^4)\approx2.49\times10^5\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}=249\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. The intercept gives $D_0$; it does not replace the slope-based activation-energy estimate.

questions.assertion: Diffusion-controlled processes (heat treatment, homogenisation, sintering, creep) are extremely temperature-sensitive.
questions.reason: D depends exponentially on 1/T, so even a small rise in temperature produces a large increase in D.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: c
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — the exponential in 1/T.
questions.concise: D depends exponentially on 1/T, so a small ΔT gives a large ΔD — hence extreme temperature sensitivity.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: diffusion-controlled processes (heat treatment, homogenisation, sintering, creep)
  are extremely temperature-sensitive.
- R is TRUE: D depends exponentially on 1/T, so even a small rise in temperature produces a
  large increase in D.

R correctly explains A. The exponential is the reason: a 100 °C rise can change D by an order
of magnitude or more, so the *rate* of every diffusion-controlled process changes enormously.
This is why a heat-treatment specification is meaningless without tight temperature control.

questions.text: Factors that raise D include:

statements.text: higher temperature
interstitial (rather than substitutional) diffusion
a lower-melting-point host lattice
removing all grain boundaries, dislocations and vacancies

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is false — vacancies, boundaries and dislocations *speed up* diffusion (short-circuit paths).
questions.concise: Higher T, interstitial mechanism and a lower-melting host all raise D — but removing defects *slows* diffusion (defects are short-circuit paths).
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: higher temperature → larger D (Arrhenius, Q25).
- Item 2 — TRUE: interstitial diffusion has lower Q_d → larger D (Q29).
- Item 3 — TRUE: a lower-melting-point host lattice is more open/less tightly bound → lower Q_d
  → larger D (the empirical melting-point correlation).
- Item 4 — FALSE: vacancies, grain boundaries and dislocations **speed up** diffusion — they are
  the short-circuit paths of Q32–Q33. Removing them would *reduce* D.

Item 4 reverses the truth. It is the counter-intuitive point that *defects help diffusion* —
exactly why annealing a heavily cold-worked metal (which removes vacancies and dislocations)
slows subsequent diffusion.

questions.text: The correct ordering of diffusion rates (fastest to slowest) is:
questions.keyExplanation: Surface > grain boundary > bulk. [P2]
questions.concise: Surface > grain boundary > bulk. Memorise this order.
questions.detailed: Diffusion is fastest along a free surface, next fastest along grain boundaries, and slowest through the bulk lattice. **(d)** is correct. The more open, disordered path has a lower activation barrier; option (b) reverses the ordering and (c) incorrectly makes the rates equal.

questions.text: Grain-boundary and surface diffusion are faster than bulk because:

statements.text: they are locally disordered regions
they offer a lower activation-energy path than the ordered lattice
they dominate transport at lower temperatures and in fine-grained material where boundary area is large
they are more densely packed than the lattice

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is the opposite (they are *less* densely packed).
questions.concise: They are disordered, lower-activation paths that dominate at low T and in fine-grained material — but they are *less* densely packed, not more.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: they are locally disordered regions.
- Item 2 — TRUE: they offer a lower activation-energy path than the ordered lattice.
- Item 3 — TRUE: they dominate transport at lower temperatures and in fine-grained material
  where boundary area per unit volume is large.
- Item 4 — FALSE: they are **less** densely packed than the lattice — that openness is *why*
  they are fast. Item 4 states the opposite.

Item 4 reverses the mechanism. Note the temperature dependence: as T falls, bulk diffusion
(collinear with a steep Q_d) collapses faster than boundary diffusion, so the short-circuit
paths take over a larger share — this is why creep and sintering are dominated by boundary
diffusion at low homologous temperature.

questions.assertion: Carbon actually diffuses *faster* in BCC iron (α-Fe) than in FCC iron (γ-Fe), even though γ-Fe dissolves far more carbon.
questions.reason: BCC has the lower packing factor (0.68 vs 0.74), giving easier atomic passage, even though its individual voids are smaller.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — lower APF gives easier passage despite smaller individual voids. This is a genuine "surprise" fact examiners like.
questions.concise: BCC's lower APF (0.68 vs 0.74) gives easier passage even though its individual voids are smaller — solubility ≠ diffusivity.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: carbon diffuses *faster* in BCC α-Fe than in FCC γ-Fe, even though γ-Fe dissolves
  far more carbon.
- R is TRUE: BCC has the lower atomic packing factor (0.68 vs 0.74), giving easier atomic
  passage even though its individual voids are smaller.

R correctly explains A. This is a genuine "surprise" fact and a favourite examiner question,
because it separates **two properties students conflate**:
```
CARBON SOLUBILITY:  FCC γ-Fe >> BCC α-Fe   (bigger voids in FCC — Ch. 2 Q42)
CARBON DIFFUSIVITY: BCC α-Fe > FCC γ-Fe   (lower APF — easier passage)
```
**Solubility is about void SIZE; diffusivity is about PACKING and barrier HEIGHT.** They point
in opposite directions here, and that is the whole point of the question.

questions.text: Match the application to its description.
tableRows: (a) joining two solid surfaces under pressure and heat, with no melting, by mutual diffusion
(b) diffusing C or N into a steel surface to raise surface hardness while keeping a tough, lower-carbon core
(c) diffusing controlled amounts of B or P into silicon to create p- and n-type regions
(d) powder compacts bonded into a solid part by solid-state diffusion across particle contacts, driven by surface-energy reduction
questions.concise: Carburizing/nitriding→surface C or N · doping→B or P into Si · sintering→powder compacts · bonding→two surfaces, no melting.
questions.detailed:
| Application | Description |
|---|---|
| **Carburizing / nitriding** | diffusing C or N into a steel surface → hard surface, tough lower-carbon core |
| **Semiconductor doping** | diffusing controlled B (p-type) or P (n-type) into silicon |
| **Sintering** | powder compacts bonded into a solid part by solid-state diffusion across particle contacts, driven by surface-energy reduction |
| **Diffusion bonding** | joining two solid surfaces under pressure and heat, **no melting**, by mutual diffusion |

Each is a real industrial application, and each is the "textbook" example of its entry. The
sintering entry's driving force (surface-energy reduction) is worth noting — it links back to
the free-surface energy of Ch. 5 Q50.

questions.text: Which statement(s) is/are correct?

statements.text: Homogenisation (Ch. 3) and recrystallisation/grain growth (Ch. 7) are, at bottom, Fick's second law run long enough to erase a concentration gradient or a high-energy grain boundary.
Carburizing raises surface hardness and wear resistance while keeping a tough core.
Sintering is driven by the reduction in surface energy as isolated particle surfaces are replaced by lower-energy grain boundaries.
Diffusion bonding requires melting the interface.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is false — diffusion bonding explicitly involves *no melting*.
questions.concise: Homogenisation and grain growth are Fick's second law run long; carburizing gives hard surface + tough core; sintering is surface-energy driven — but diffusion bonding involves NO melting.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: homogenisation (erasing a concentration gradient) and recrystallisation/grain
  growth (erasing high-energy boundaries) are, at bottom, Fick's second law run long enough.
- Item 2 — TRUE: carburizing raises surface hardness and wear resistance while keeping a tough,
  lower-carbon core.
- Item 3 — TRUE: sintering is driven by the reduction in surface energy as isolated particle
  surfaces are replaced by lower-energy grain boundaries.
- Item 4 — FALSE: diffusion bonding explicitly involves **no melting** — that is what
  distinguishes it from welding/casting. Solid-state diffusion alone joins the surfaces.

Item 4 is the false member, and it contradicts the very definition in Q35. Item 1 is a nice
synthesis worth remembering: it reframes two earlier-chapter processes as instances of the
second law, which is exactly how diffusion "closes" the course.

questions.text: The direct exchange mechanism — two neighbouring atoms swapping positions — is practically never observed in pure metals at ordinary temperatures because:

options.label: a
options.text: it requires a vacant lattice site to be present first

options.label: b
options.text: both atoms must squeeze past their neighbours simultaneously, so the transient lattice distortion makes the energy barrier prohibitively large

options.label: c
options.text: it is forbidden by the symmetry of every crystal structure

options.label: d
options.text: it can only operate at grain boundaries, never in the lattice

questions.keyExplanation: Simultaneous swapping forces both atoms through a crowded saddle point, so direct exchange has a prohibitively high activation energy.
questions.concise: Direct exchange forces both atoms through a crowded saddle point at once — the distortion makes the barrier prohibitive.
questions.detailed: Direct exchange requires two neighbouring atoms to move past one another simultaneously, producing a highly crowded transition configuration and a prohibitively large activation barrier. **(b)** is correct. A vacancy is not required for direct exchange; that is a different mechanism.

questions.text: In the ring (collective) mechanism, a small group of atoms rotates cooperatively around a closed path, so atoms change places without any vacancy being involved.
questions.keyExplanation: The ring mechanism is a cooperative rotation of a group of atoms — no vacancy is required.
questions.concise: The ring mechanism is a cooperative rotation of a group of atoms — no vacancy is involved.
questions.detailed:
In the **ring (collective) mechanism** several atoms move simultaneously around a closed loop, each yielding its position to the next, so a net displacement occurs with **no vacancy required**. It was proposed for close-packed metals where a single direct swap (Q37) is too costly, and computer simulations find it mainly in hcp metals such as Cd and Zn.
- (b) is false: the defining feature of the ring mechanism is precisely that it is vacancy-free.

questions.text: For a substitutional alloy diffusing by the vacancy mechanism, the measured activation energy Q_d is:

options.label: a
options.text: the migration energy alone — the energy to move an atom into an adjacent vacancy

options.label: c
options.text: the sum of the vacancy formation energy and the atom migration energy

options.label: d
options.text: the sum of the vacancy formation energy and the elastic strain energy of an interstitial atom

questions.keyExplanation: For the vacancy mechanism Q_d = vacancy formation energy + atom migration energy.
questions.concise: For the vacancy mechanism Q_d = vacancy formation energy + migration energy.
questions.detailed:
- The atom can only jump if a vacancy is present (cost: the formation energy that fixes the equilibrium vacancy concentration) and it must then surmount the migration barrier to move into it.
- The two barriers act in series: **Q_d = Q_v + Q_m**, which is why Q_d for substitutional self-diffusion is roughly 0.5–0.7 of the melting-point energy.
- (a) is Q_m alone — measurable, say, by internal friction, and smaller than Q_d.
- (b) is Q_v alone — it sets vacancy availability, not the jump barrier.
- (d) mixes in an interstitial concept that does not apply to substitutional diffusion.

questions.assertion: Migration of inert markers in an interdiffusion couple is taken as evidence that substitutional diffusion proceeds by the vacancy mechanism.
questions.reason: Direct exchange of two neighbouring atoms would require a very large lattice distortion and therefore an impractically high activation energy.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true, but R explains why direct exchange is rare, not why marker movement proves the vacancy mechanism.
questions.concise: Both true, but R explains why direct exchange is rare, not why marker motion proves the vacancy mechanism.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: migration of inert markers welded at the interface is the classic evidence that substitutional diffusion runs on a vacancy counterflux.
- R is TRUE: direct exchange would demand an impractically large lattice distortion.
- But R answers a different question. The evidence lies in the **unequal intrinsic diffusivities** — a net vacancy flux to one side drags the lattice past the markers. The mere rarity of exchange does not, by itself, prove the vacancy route.
This is the favourite assertion–reason trap: a true, relevant-sounding reason that does not logically produce the assertion.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the Kirkendall effect is/are correct?

statements.text: It arises because the intrinsic diffusivities of the two components of the couple are generally unequal.
Inert markers welded at the original interface migrate relative to the ends of the couple.
The chemical (interdiffusion) coefficient is a Darken-weighted combination of the two intrinsic coefficients, not either intrinsic coefficient alone.
Markers move toward the side containing the slower-diffusing component.

questions.keyExplanation: Items 1, 2 and 3 are correct; markers move toward the side of the *faster*-diffusing component, so item 4 is false.
questions.concise: Items 1–3 correct; markers move toward the *faster*-diffusing side, so item 4 reverses the direction.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: unequal intrinsic diffusivities create a compensating net vacancy flux — the origin of the effect.
- Item 2 — TRUE: that migration of markers *is* the Kirkendall effect.
- Item 3 — TRUE: Darken's relation D̃ = N_B D_A + N_A D_B shows the chemical diffusivity mixes both intrinsic coefficients.
- Item 4 — FALSE: markers move toward the side of the **faster**-diffusing component (worked out in Q42).

Item 4 is the [P2] inversion — the single most common Kirkendall slip. Note also that if D_A = D_B exactly, there is no vacancy counterflow and no marker movement at all.

questions.text: In the classic Cu–brass diffusion couple, zinc is the faster diffuser and leaves the brass side. Inert markers welded at the original interface:

options.label: a
options.text: remain fixed, because both components are substitutional

options.label: b
options.text: move toward the copper side, following the net zinc flux

options.label: c
options.text: move toward the brass side, because the brass loses lattice sites as the faster-diffusing zinc departs

options.label: d
options.text: move randomly, since marker motion is not reproducible

questions.keyExplanation: Brass loses lattice sites as the faster-diffusing Zn departs, so the marker plane migrates toward the brass side.
questions.concise: Markers move toward the brass — the side losing lattice sites as Zn departs.
questions.detailed:
- Zn (the faster diffuser) leaves the brass → net atomic flux brass → Cu.
- Lattice planes must therefore be **destroyed** on the brass side and **created** on the Cu side.
- Markers are welded to lattice planes, so they drift toward the brass; Kirkendall voids likewise appear on the brass side.
- (b) reverses the direction; (a) and (d) are simply false.
**Rule to memorise:** markers move toward the side that *contains the faster-diffusing species* — the side that shrinks.

questions.assertion: In a fine-grained polycrystalline metal, the grain boundaries carry a larger fraction of the total diffusion flux at 400 °C than at 1000 °C.
questions.reason: Grain-boundary diffusion has a lower activation energy than lattice diffusion, so it decreases more slowly as the temperature falls.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — the lower boundary activation energy is exactly why boundary transport falls off more slowly on cooling.
questions.concise: Both true — lower Q_gb means boundary flux falls off more slowly on cooling, so its share grows.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: at 400 °C the boundaries carry a larger fraction of the total flux than at 1000 °C.
- R is TRUE: grain-boundary diffusion has a lower activation energy than lattice diffusion.
- R correctly explains A: with D = D₀ exp(−Q_d/RT), the path with the **smaller Q_d** loses less on cooling, so the ratio D_gb/D_lattice rises steadily as T falls. Below the so-called crossover temperature the boundaries dominate — which is why creep and sintering at low homologous temperature are boundary-controlled.

questions.text: Match the diffusion path or process to its description.
tableRows: (a) vacancy transport along grain boundaries; creep rate strongly grain-size dependent, ∝ 1/d³
(b) lower activation energy; carries the larger share of flux at low temperature and in fine-grained material
(c) highest activation energy; slowest path, but dominates the total flux at high temperature
(d) fast one-dimensional transport along the disordered dislocation cores in cold-worked metal
questions.keyExplanation: 1-c, 2-b, 3-d, 4-a: bulk is fastest at high T, boundaries at low T, pipes are 1-D cores, Coble creep runs along boundaries (rate ∝ 1/d³).
questions.concise: Bulk→highest Q_d, high-T dominated; boundary→low-T; pipe→1-D dislocation cores; Coble creep→boundary vacancy flux, rate ∝ 1/d³.
questions.detailed:
- **Bulk (lattice) diffusion** → (c): highest activation energy; dominates total flux at high temperature.
- **Grain-boundary diffusion** → (b): lower activation energy; dominates at low temperature and in fine-grained material.
- **Dislocation pipe diffusion** → (d): fast one-dimensional transport along disordered cores, important in cold-worked metals.
- **Coble creep** → (a): diffusion creep with the vacancy flux running along grain boundaries; rate ∝ σ/d³.
Watch the pairing: **Nabarro–Herring creep** is the lattice counterpart (vacancy flux through grain interiors, rate ∝ 1/d²) — do not cross the two.

questions.text: Hydrogen permeates a palladium membrane 3 mm thick under steady state. The upstream face is held at C₁ = 1.2 mol/m³, the downstream face at effectively zero, and D = 5×10⁻¹⁰ m²/s. The steady-state flux is:
questions.keyExplanation: J = D(C₁ − C₂)/L = 5×10⁻¹⁰ × 1.2/(3×10⁻³) = 2×10⁻⁷ mol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ — the mm→m conversion is the trap.
questions.detailed: For steady permeation, J = D(C₁ − C₂)/L. With L = 3 × 10⁻³ m, J = (5 × 10⁻¹⁰)(1.2)/(3 × 10⁻³) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ mol·m⁻²·s⁻¹. **(b)** is correct. Option (a) omits the millimetre-to-metre conversion; the other options use an incorrect length or operation.

questions.text: The diffusion coefficient of a substitutional solute in copper is 1.0×10⁻¹² m²/s at 500 °C. Given Q_d = 120 kJ/mol, D at 600 °C is closest to:
questions.keyExplanation: D₂/D₁ = exp[(Q_d/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)] = exp(2.14) ≈ 8.5, so D₂ ≈ 8.5×10⁻¹² m²/s.
questions.concise: D(600 °C) ≈ 8.5×10⁻¹² m²/s — an 8.5-fold rise for +100 K.
questions.detailed: Using D₂/D₁ = exp[(Q_d/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)] with T₁ = 773 K and T₂ = 873 K gives an exponent of about 2.14, so D₂/D₁ ≈ 8.5. Thus D₂ ≈ 8.5 × 10⁻¹² m²/s and **(c)** is correct.

questions.text: The diffusion coefficient of carbon in γ-Fe is 2.8×10⁻¹² m²/s at 800 °C and 3.4×10⁻¹¹ m²/s at 1000 °C. The activation energy Q_d is closest to:
questions.concise: Q_d = R ln(D₂/D₁)/(1/T₁ − 1/T₂) ≈ 142 kJ/mol — the textbook value for C in γ-Fe.
questions.detailed: The activation energy is Q_d = R ln(D₂/D₁)/(1/T₁ − 1/T₂). Here D₂/D₁ ≈ 12.1 and the reciprocal-temperature difference is 1.464 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, giving Q_d ≈ 142 kJ/mol. **(b)** is correct. The logarithm of the diffusivity ratio is essential.

questions.text: A steel initially at $C_0=0.2$ wt% C is carburized with surface concentration held at $C_s=1.0$ wt% C. For $D=1.0\times10^{-11}$ m$^2$/s, find the carbon concentration at $x=0.3$ mm after 1 h. Use $\operatorname{erf}(0.79)\approx0.736$.
questions.keyExplanation: For constant surface concentration in a semi-infinite solid, $(C_x-C_0)/(C_s-C_0)=1-\operatorname{erf}(x/(2\sqrt{Dt}))$. Here $x/(2\sqrt{Dt})\approx0.79$, so $C_x=0.2+(1-0.736)(1.0-0.2)\approx0.411$ wt% C.
questions.concise: Use the complementary error function: $C_x=C_0+(C_s-C_0)[1-\operatorname{erf}(z)]\approx0.41$ wt% C.
questions.detailed: Convert $x=0.3$ mm to $3.0\times10^{-4}$ m and $t=1$ h to 3600 s. Then $\sqrt{Dt}=\sqrt{1.0\times10^{-11}\times3600}=1.90\times10^{-4}$ m and $z=x/(2\sqrt{Dt})\approx0.79$. The semi-infinite, fixed-surface solution gives $C_x=C_0+(C_s-C_0)[1-\operatorname{erf}(z)]=0.2+0.8(1-0.736)\approx0.411$ wt% C. Option a results from using $x$ in millimetres with $D$ in m$^2$/s; option b is the arithmetic midpoint of $C_0$ and $C_s$ and ignores the error-function factor; option c confuses the argument $z$ with a carbon concentration. The result is valid under the stated semi-infinite and constant-surface assumptions.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the √(Dt) scaling of case depth is/are correct?

statements.text: Doubling the treatment time at the same temperature increases the case depth by a factor √2 only.
Halving the required case depth reduces the treatment time to one quarter.
Case depth is directly proportional to the product Dt.
Quadrupling the treatment time doubles the case depth.

questions.keyExplanation: Items 1, 2 and 4 follow from depth ∝ √(Dt); item 3 wrongly makes depth linear in Dt.
questions.concise: Items 1, 2 and 4 all follow from depth ∝ √(Dt); item 3 wrongly makes depth linear in Dt.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: depth ∝ √t, so 2× time buys only √2 × depth.
- Item 2 — TRUE: t ∝ depth², so half the depth costs one quarter of the time.
- Item 3 — FALSE: depth ∝ √(Dt), **not** Dt — this is the trap statement.
- Item 4 — TRUE: 4× time doubles the depth.
One relation generates everything: **t ∝ depth²** at fixed D.

questions.text: An exam error-function table gives erf(0.2) = 0.2227, erf(0.4) = 0.4284, erf(0.6) = 0.6039, erf(0.8) = 0.7421. In a carburizing problem the normalised concentration (C_x − C₀)/(C_s − C₀) equals 0.5716. The corresponding value of z = x/(2√(Dt)) is:
questions.keyExplanation: erf(z) = 1 − 0.5716 = 0.4284, and the table gives erf(0.4) = 0.4284, so z = 0.40.
questions.concise: erf(z) = 1 − 0.5716 = 0.4284, and the table gives erf(0.4) = 0.4284, so z = 0.40.
questions.detailed: The normalised concentration is 0.5716 = 1 − erf(z), so erf(z) = 0.4284. The supplied table gives erf(0.4) = 0.4284; therefore z = 0.40 and **(d)** is correct.

questions.text: Two points on an Arrhenius plot of a substitutional diffusivity are (1/T = 1.0×10⁻³ K⁻¹, ln D = −30.0) and (1/T = 1.2×10⁻³ K⁻¹, ln D = −34.8). The activation energy Q_d is closest to:
questions.keyExplanation: Slope = −4.8/(0.2×10⁻³) = −24,000 K, hence Q_d = −slope × R ≈ 200 kJ/mol.
questions.concise: Slope = −4.8/(0.2×10⁻³) = −24,000 K, hence Q_d = −slope × R ≈ 200 kJ/mol.
questions.detailed: The Arrhenius-plot slope is ΔlnD/Δ(1/T) = −4.8/(0.2 × 10⁻³) = −24,000 K. Hence Q_d = −slope × R ≈ 24,000 × 8.314 = 2.0 × 10⁵ J/mol = 200 kJ/mol. **(d)** is correct.

questions.text: A gas permeates a metal membrane to a steady-state flux J. If the membrane is made twice as thick while both face concentrations and the temperature are unchanged, the new steady-state flux is:
questions.keyExplanation: J = D(C₁ − C₂)/L, so doubling L halves the steady-state flux.
questions.concise: J = DΔC/L, so doubling the thickness halves the steady-state flux.
questions.detailed: At steady state, J = D(C₁ − C₂)/L. Doubling the membrane thickness halves the concentration gradient and therefore halves the flux. **(b)** is correct. The flux is inversely proportional to thickness.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about short-circuit diffusion paths is/are correct?

statements.text: Grain-boundary diffusion has a lower activation energy than lattice diffusion.
In a fine-grained material the boundaries carry a larger share of the total transport than in a coarse-grained one at the same temperature.
Dislocation cores provide a fast one-dimensional pipe diffusion path.
Near the melting point, short-circuit paths dominate the total flux in every polycrystalline metal.

questions.keyExplanation: Items 1, 2 and 3 are correct; item 4 is false — near T_m the lattice carries most of the flux.
questions.concise: Items 1–3 correct; near T_m the *lattice* dominates, so item 4 reverses the temperature trend.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: the disordered boundary region offers a lower barrier than the ordered lattice.
- Item 2 — TRUE: finer grains means more boundary area per unit volume, hence a larger boundary share.
- Item 3 — TRUE: dislocation cores are fast **one-dimensional** pipe paths, strongest in cold-worked metals.
- Item 4 — FALSE: at high homologous temperature bulk diffusion is fast enough to dominate; short circuits take over as temperature **falls**.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about activation energies for diffusion is/are correct?

statements.text: Q_d for self-diffusion tends to be larger in metals with higher melting points.
Q_d for grain-boundary diffusion is smaller than for lattice diffusion.
Q_d measures the height of the migration barrier, while the jump-frequency and geometric factors sit in D₀.
A larger Q_d makes D less sensitive to temperature changes.

questions.keyExplanation: Items 1, 2 and 3 are correct; a larger Q_d makes D *more* temperature-sensitive, not less.
questions.concise: Items 1–3 correct; a larger Q_d makes D *more* temperature-sensitive, not less.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: higher melting point means stronger binding and larger Q_v + Q_m — the classic empirical correlation.
- Item 2 — TRUE: the open, disordered boundary path has a lower barrier than the perfect lattice.
- Item 3 — TRUE: Q_d is the barrier height; the attempt frequency and geometric factors sit in D₀.
- Item 4 — FALSE: higher Q_d means a **steeper** ln D vs 1/T line, i.e. greater temperature sensitivity — the logic of Q29–Q30.

questions.text: A thin radioactive tracer layer of areal dose M is sandwiched between two half-specimens and annealed. The thin-film (instantaneous source) solution of Fick's second law is:
questions.keyExplanation: The thin-film solution is a Gaussian with the M/(2√(πDt)) prefactor that decays as the profile broadens.
questions.concise: The thin-film solution is a Gaussian whose 1/√(Dt) prefactor decays as the profile broadens.
questions.detailed: For an instantaneous thin tracer layer with conserved areal dose M, the concentration profile is a spreading Gaussian: C(x,t) = M/[2√(πDt)] exp[−x²/(4Dt)]. **(c)** is correct. Its prefactor decreases as √t increases, preserving the integrated tracer dose; the other options have the wrong profile or time dependence.

questions.text: The diffusion coefficient of carbon in γ-Fe at 1000 °C is 3×10⁻¹¹ m²/s. Expressed in cm²/s this is:
questions.keyExplanation: 1 m² = 10⁴ cm², so 3×10⁻¹¹ m²/s = 3×10⁻¹¹ × 10⁴ = 3×10⁻⁷ cm²/s.
questions.concise: 1 m² = 10⁴ cm², so 3×10⁻¹¹ m²/s = 3×10⁻⁷ cm²/s.
questions.detailed: Since 1 m = 100 cm, 1 m² = 10⁴ cm². Therefore 3 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s = 3 × 10⁻⁷ cm²/s, so **(c)** is correct. Area conversion squares the length factor.
